```","language":"none"}],"mentions":[{"end":21,"start":14,"username":"blocks"},{"end":60,"start":47,"username":"nousresearch"},{"end":17,"start":7,"username":"nykdotdev"}],"urls":[{"text":"buzz.xyz"},{"text":"https://nyk.dev/#newsletter"},{"text":"https://t.me/+GJ-FEpzcZrtmMTky"},{"text":"https://nyk.dev/#newsletter"},{"text":"https://t.me/+GJ-FEpzcZrtmMTky"}]},"media_entities":["3_2082312161284804608","3_2082312233506533376","3_2082312303358377984","3_2082312378956619776"],"plain_text":"In July 2026, @blocks Buzz plus Hermes Agent ( @nousresearch ) shifted the job: from prompts in chat to a 5-layer room system.
Teams blame the chat product, but in practice, the failure lies in cloning the agent OS into every message surface.
Here is the exact 5-layer runbook: room identity, agent keypair, ACP harness, Hermes config, and control gates. 
Save this checklist if you want room work to finish without a second install.
 
Why the default approach fails
The default approach is:
pick a chat product
paste an API key into that product's agent panel
hope the product's runtime is "good enough"
when it is not, copy the whole agent into the next product
That path fails in four predictable ways.
Identity drift. Humans keep one identity. Agents get a new one per app. Mentions, audit, and blame stop matching.
Tool policy drift. Editor approvals, terminal allowlists, and MCP servers get reimplemented per surface. Safety becomes folklore.
Memory drift. The same person teaches three installs the same preferences. None of them compound.
Transport confusion. People try to fix a missing room protocol by forking the agent, or fix a weak agent by bolting more chat features onto it.

The 5-layer room stack
Think of a human mention becoming a model turn as five seats, not five products.
Room - Buzz community, channels, signed events
Agent identity - dedicated Nostr keypair, membership, not your human key
Transport - buzz-acp or Desktop harness speaking ACP over stdio
Agent OS - Hermes config, model route, skills, memory, toolsets
Control gates - owner-only, worker count, tool scope, restart behavior

Skip a layer, and you get a demo.
 Keep all five and you get a room teammate with a receipt trail.

Layer 1 - Buzz is the room, not the brain
Buzz is a self-hostable workspace from Block where humans and AI agents share the same rooms. It is built on Nostr. Messages, reactions, workflow steps, review approvals, and git events land as signed events in one log. Apache 2.0. Hosted at buzz.xyz or run your own relay.
That design choice is the room layer: one community URL as workspace boundary, the same identity model for people and processes, one event shape for search and audit.
Buzz is not your personal agent OS. Its agent vision is protocol-native: ACP for the agent interface, MCP for tools, no custom wire format coupling.
Use Buzz when you need shared, signed, multi-party context. Do not use it as a substitute for Hermes memory, cron, or skill learning.
Anti-pattern: stuffing the entire personal assistant into the Desktop default runtime with no boundary between room teammate and laptop brain.
Layer 2 - Give the agent its own keypair
Hermes docs and the buzz-acp README say the same thing in plain language: mint a dedicated Nostr keypair for the agent. Do not reuse a human keypair. Register that pubkey as a relay member. Add that identity only to the channels where it should work.
Channel membership is the access boundary. The bridge discovers channels where the agent is a member and auto-subscribes when membership changes. Hermes does not need a second channel allowlist of its own.
This is the seat most demos skip. They paste one human nsec into the harness, then wonder why audit trails look haunted.
You should see:
agent pubkey distinct from your personal pubkey
agent listed as a channel member in the rooms you chose
no agent membership in rooms you did not intend
Standing rule: one agent identity per role. If you later need a coder and a triage voice, mint two keypairs. Do not overload one room identity until the first role is boringly reliable.
Layer 3 - ACP is the wire, not a second install
Agent Client Protocol (ACP) is how hosts talk to an agent over stdio: chat, tools, diffs, terminals, approvals. Hermes runs as an ACP server with hermes acp after the ACP extra is installed.
Buzz's harness side is buzz-acp. The public diagram is:
, not a second Hermes installation. The subprocess uses the same Hermes configuration, credentials, memory, skills, and state as hermes on that host.
 
 
 
Relay bridge (buzz-acp) - join Buzz channels as an agent identity, often on a server
Buzz Desktop managed runtime - local preset or custom harness that spawns Hermes for Desktop-managed agents
Desktop can discover Hermes as a preset when hermes / hermes-acp is on PATH. You can also register a custom harness that points at hermes with args ["acp"] (or a profile-scoped command).
Anti-pattern: installing a second Hermes tree "for Buzz" so Desktop and CLI diverge. That recreates the clone problem inside your home directory.
Layer 4 - Hermes stays the agent OS
Hermes Agent is Nous Research's self-improving agent harness: skills from experience, memory nudges, session search, subagents, multi-platform gateway, model-agnostic providers.
When you put Hermes behind Buzz, you are choosing one place for provider route, skills, durable memory policy, toolset enable/disable, and profiles when roles must isolate.
ACP mode still uses the normal Hermes config paths. A host that owns MCP can set HERMES_ACP_SKIP_CONFIGURED_MCP=1 so global MCP does not delay initialize, while session MCP still registers.
That matters for room work. Buzz can supply room-scoped tools. Hermes should not silently pull every laptop MCP into a shared channel.
Anti-pattern: treating Desktop's managed agent as a full replacement for Hermes profiles, skill iteration, and Hermes doctor. 
Desktop is the room UI. 
Hermes is still the OS.
Layer 5 - Control gates before clever prompts
This is the layer that decides whether the stack is a teammate or a liability.
Owner-only is the default for a reason
Buzz creates agents with Who can talk to this agent set to Owner only. Hermes docs say leave it there when the runtime is Hermes.
Why: the hermes-acp toolset includes terminal and code execution. On the Buzz path, the bridge can answer permission requests with allow_once instead of showing a human prompt. Hermes docs state that the path can run shell commands on the host without a prompt. Selecting Anyone hands that shell access to every author who can reach the channel.
Owner-only is not etiquette. It is the shell boundary for a first deployment.
One worker while you prove the room
Buzz ACP defaults lean toward a small worker pool. For a private proof, set managed-agent parallelism to 1, keep start-on-launch off until the mention path is clean, and confirm the process tree shows one ACP child for that agent. Parallelism is a scaling knob, not a reliability free lunch.
Scope tools to the room job
If the room agent only needs channel context and a narrow MCP set, disable the broad coding toolset on that Hermes profile or harness path. Room evidence is untrusted shared text. Do not auto-promote channel content into durable memory. Require owner approval for external or irreversible actions.
Restart behavior
A good room agent answers a live owner mention once. It does not replay stale mentions into duplicate replies after Desktop restarts. Test restart before you trust the agent with real work.
Mechanism dive - why ACP beats another bot SDK
The comparison people make is wrong.
They compare "Buzz agents" to "Slack bots" to "Discord bots" and pick a UI.
The real comparison is three approaches:
Product-native bot - optimizes for a fast demo. You pay later with second memory, second tools, second identity.
Fork Hermes into the app - optimizes for local control. You pay later with merge debt and upgrade pain.
ACP bridge - optimizes for one agent OS plus room transport. You pay with harness config and gate discipline.
ACP wins when three conditions hold:
The agent already has a better learning loop and tool policy than the chat product's built-in runtime.
The room product already has better multi-party identity and audit than a DM bot.
You refuse to maintain two copies of skills and memory.
Buzz chose Nostr for multi-agent identity. Hermes chose ACP so hosts can reuse one runtime. The bridge is the product of those two decisions, not a third framework.
Formula for the path:
 
-> ACP session (cwd, model, tools)
-> Hermes turn (skills, memory policy, tool calls)
-> signed reply event in the same room log
If any arrow is "paste a new system prompt in a different product," you fell off the stack.
Worked example - one dogfood week without a fork
Week shape, sanitized to what is public and reproducible.
Day 0 - install surfaces
Clone or install Buzz. Run local relay or join a hosted community.
Install Hermes normally. Install ACP extra. Run hermes acp - check.
Confirm command -v hermes (and hermes-acp if present).
Day 1 - identities
Human identity for you.
Separate agent keypair via buzz-admin generate-key / Desktop agent create flow.
Agent becomes member of one private test channel only.
Day 2 - transport
Path A: buzz-acp with BUZZ_ACP_AGENT_COMMAND=hermes and BUZZ_ACP_AGENT_ARGS=acp.
Path B: Buzz Desktop custom harness or preset Hermes runtime pointing at the same install.
Owner-only respond gate on.
Day 3 - smoke
Owner mention returns one coherent reply.
Non-owner mention does not fire the agent.
Process tree shows the expected single worker for that managed agent.
No surprise tool calls outside the room job.
Day 4-7 - real room work
Post concrete tasks in the private channel (triage notes, design questions, checklist drafts).
Require the agent to answer with receipts in-thread, not vibes.
Keep heartbeat and multi-worker experiments off until three clean owner turns land.
What I refused that week: fork Buzz, fork Hermes, or stand up a second Hermes home only for the room. The only custom piece was harness configuration and agent membership.
What broke first was never the model brand. It was layer 5: parallelism too high, wrong respond-to, agent not a channel member. Fix the gates before you rewrite prompts.
ACP Room Bridge Checklist
Use this when: you already run Hermes, you want a multi-party room, and you refuse a second agent install.
Install both products as themselves - Buzz for the room, Hermes for the agent OS. No fork plan on day one.
Mint a dedicated agent keypair - never reuse the human nsec.
Register membership - agent is a relay member and a member of only the intended channels.
Choose one transport path - buzz-acp relay bridge or Desktop managed/custom harness. Document which.
Point the harness at existing Hermes - hermes acp / hermes-acp, same config home you already trust.
Set Owner only - leave it there while terminal tools exist on the path.
Set parallelism to 1 for the proof window.
Disable start-on-launch and heartbeat until smoke is green.
Scope tools - room MCP in, broad coding out, until the job needs hands.
Run the accept test - owner mention once, non-owner silence, restart without duplicate reply.
Write the rollback - stop agent, kill ACP children, remove membership, keep Hermes install intact.
Only then expand channels, tools, or workers.
You should see:
one Hermes install serving CLI and room
one agent pubkey with narrow membership
one clean owner-triggered reply path
zero "which bot is this?" identity confusion
 
Failure modes to watch for
1. Human keypair reuse
Audit becomes meaningless. Fix: mint agent keys and rotate the leaked human key if it was ever pasted into a harness env.
2. Anyone can talk
You offered host shell to the channel. Fix: Owner only. Re-read the Hermes Buzz Desktop warning before you change it.
3. Second Hermes install for Buzz
Skills and memory diverge in a week. Fix: custom harness args into the primary install or a named Hermes profile, not a parallel tree you forget to update.
4. Agent not in the channel
Harness discovers zero channels. Fix: membership first, prompts second.
5. Parallelism theater
Ten workers, duplicate replies, confusing process trees. Fix: one worker until three clean days.
6. Treating room text as trusted memory
Prompt injection with better UX. Fix: room content is evidence. Durable memory writes stay owner-gated.
7. Desktop offline observer trap
Ephemeral activity frames need Desktop online for the turn if you rely on the live activity log. Fix: do not treat missing observer UI as "agent is dead" without checking the process and channel reply.
8. Scope bleed across communities
Global Desktop agents can appear in more than one community. Fix: separate agents/runtimes per trust boundary when rooms have different risk.
When not to use this
Skip the Buzz Hermes ACP bridge when:
you only need a single-player coding agent in an editor (use Hermes ACP in Zed/VS Code directly)
you do not want any agent with terminal reach on a shared host
your "room" is a broadcast marketing channel (wrong product class)
you need a fully productized, zero-ops bot and refuse to own relay or Desktop process hygiene
the job is pure Hermes gateway chat (Telegram/Discord/etc.) with no multi-party signed workspace requirement
Honest alternative: stay in Hermes CLI + gateway until the pain is specifically shared room identity and audit, not "I want a shinier sidebar."
Setting this up over 2 weeks
Week 1 - proof
Day 1-2: installs, keys, one private channel
Day 3: transport + owner-only + one worker
Day 4-5: smoke and restart tests
Day 6-7: three real owner tasks, write what broke
Week 2 - harden
Narrow toolset permanently for the room role
Add a second channel only if membership rules stay clear
Document harness JSON or env in your operator notes (not in the public channel)
Decide profile split: default Hermes vs room-scoped profile
Still no fork of Buzz or Hermes unless a gate cannot be configured upstream
Do not require full orchestra day one. One private channel and one agent is enough to learn the stack.
Measuring whether it still earns rent
Monthly audit, 20 minutes:
Identity - Agent pubkeys still dedicated? any human key reuse?
Membership - channel list still minimal?
Workers - process tree still matches intended parallelism?
Respond-to - still owner-only for shell-capable runtimes?
Duplicate rate - any double replies after restart?
Tool scope - any new MCP or coding tools added only for a demo?
Use count - if the room agent is unused for two weeks, stop it. Idle privileged bridges are not free.
Keep a simple log: date, task, pass/fail, gate that failed. The log is more valuable than another system prompt tweak.
Honest limits (July 2026)
Buzz is young as a public product surface. Expect sharp edges on membership UX, multi-tenant hosting, and Desktop process management. Prefer upstream issues over silent forks.
Hermes ACP toolsets are editor-shaped by default. Room jobs may need intentional narrowing.
Approval UX on the Buzz Desktop path is not the same as editor approval prompts. Read the owner-only section as binding ops advice, not optional polish.
This article is an operator bridge pattern. It is not a claim that Buzz replaces Hermes gateway platforms, or that Hermes replaces Buzz rooms.
No invented latency or cost numbers here. Measure your own mention-to-reply time after smoke is green.
Closing
Chat products will keep shipping "agents."
That is fine.
The bottleneck is not model access. The bottleneck is forking a new agent personality into every surface that can render a message list.
Buzz gives you a room with signed multi-party identity. Hermes gives you an agent OS that already learns. ACP is the wire that keeps them from becoming two half-broken copies of each other.
Your next action: run the ACP Room Bridge Checklist on one private channel this week.
If you could instrument one bottleneck this week, which layer would you pick first: identity, harness, Hermes config, or the owner-only gate?
